L33: # Hypersurfaces with degenerate duals and the Geometric Complexity Theory Program Thanks:  Landsberg supported by NSF grant DMS-0805782.
L34: NR supported by the French National Research Agency (ANR-09-JCJC-0102-01)
L35: 
L36: J.M. Landsberg, Laurent Manivel and Nicolas Ressayre Email address: jml@math.tamu.edu, laurent.manivel@ujf-grenoble.fr, ressayre@math.univ-montp2.fr
L37: 
L38: Date: April 2010
L39: ###### Abstract.
L40: We determine set-theoretic defining equations for the variety $Dual_{k,d,N}\subset\mathbb{P}(S^{d}\mathbb{C}^{N})$ of hypersurfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{C}^{N}$ that have dual variety of dimension at most $k$.
L41: We apply these equations to the Mulmuley-Sohoni variety $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}\subset\mathbb{P}(S^{n}\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}})$, showing it is an irreducible component of the variety of hypersurfaces of degree $n$ in $\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}}$ with dual of dimension at most $2n-2$. We establish additional geometric properties of the Mulmuley-Sohoni variety and prove a quadratic lower bound for the determinental border-complexity of the permanent.
L42: ## 1. Introduction
L43: A classical problem in linear algebra is to determine or bound the smallest integer $n$ such that the permanent of an $m\times m$ matrix may be realized as a linear projection of the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix. L. Valiant [cite21†7 ] proposed using this problem as an algebraic analog of the problem of comparing the complexity classes $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{NP}$. Call this value of $n$, $dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$.
L44: He conjectured that $dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$ grows faster than any polynomial in $m$. The best known lower bound is $dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2}$, which was proved in [cite22†3 ].
L45: The definition of $dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$ may be rephrased as follows: let $\ell$ be a linear coordinate on $\mathbb{C}$, let $\mathbb{C}\oplus M_{m}(\mathbb{C})\subset M_{n}(\mathbb{C})$, be any linear inclusion, where $M_{n}(\mathbb{C})$ denotes the space of complex $n\times n$ matrices; then $dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$ is the smallest $n$ such that $\ell^{n-m}\operatorname{perm}_{m}\in\operatorname{End}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))\cdot\operatorname{det}_{n}$.
L46: Here $u\in\operatorname{End}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))$ acts by $(u\cdot\operatorname{det}_{n})(M):=\operatorname{det}_{n}(u(M))$.
L47: K. Mulmuley and M. Sohoni [cite23†4 , cite24†5 ], have proposed to study the function $\overline{dc}(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$, which is the smallest $n$ such that $[\ell^{n-m}\operatorname{perm}_{m}]$ is contained in the orbit closure $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}\subset\mathbb{P}(S^{n}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))^{*})$. Here $S^{n}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))^{*}$ denotes the homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ on $M_{n}(\mathbb{C})$. The best known lower bound on this function had been linear.
L48: Note that $\overline{dc}(\operatorname{perm}_{m})\leq dc(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$, the potential difference being the added flexibility of limiting polynomials in $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$ that are not in $End(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]$. Our main result about $\overline{dc}(\operatorname{perm}_{m})$ is the following quadratic bound.
L49: ###### Theorem 1.0.1.
L50: 
L51: $\overline{dc}(\operatorname{perm}_{m})\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2}$.
L52: 
L53: Consider the ideal of regular functions on $S^{n}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C})^{*})$ that are zero on $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$. We construct an explicit sub-$GL_{n^{2}}$-module $V_{n}$ in this ideal which has the following properties.
L54: ###### Theorem 1.0.2.
L55: 
L56:   1. (1)
L57: 
L58: The $GL_{n^{2}}$-module $V_{n}$ contains an irreducible module of highest weight
L59: 
L60:  | $$n(n-1)(n-2)\omega_{1}+(2n^{2}-4n-1)\omega_{2}+2\omega_{2n+1}$$  |
L61: 
L62: and $V_{n}$ is a subspace of the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $n(n-1)$ on $S^{n}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))^{*}$.
L63: 
L64:   2. (2)
L65: 
L66: The variety $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$ is an irreducible component of the zero locus ${\mathcal{D}}_{n}$ of $V_{n}$.
L67: Theorem cite25†1.0.2 provides the first explicit module of equations in the ideal of $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$. However $\operatorname{dim}({\mathcal{D}}_{n})$ grows exponentially with $n$, whereas $\operatorname{dim}(\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]})$ is on the order of $n^{4}$. In particular, ${\mathcal{D}}_{n}$ has other irreducible components, one of which is described in §4.
L68: A more precise statement than Theorem cite25†1.0.2 is Theorem cite26†3.1.1 , which implies that our equations provide a full set of local equations of $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$ around $[\det_{n}]$.
L69: One can similarly define $dc(P),\overline{dc}(P)$ for an arbitrary polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ in $N$ variables. Such a polynomial, if nonzero, defines a hypersurface $Z(P)\subset\mathbb{P}^{N-1}$. If $P$ is reduced, the Zariski closure of the set of tangent hyperplanes to this hypersurface is a subvariety $Z(P)^{*}$ of the dual projective space, called the dual variety of $Z(P)$. For generic such $P$, $Z(P)^{*}$ is a hypersurface.
L70: ###### Theorem 1.0.3.
L71: 
L72: For any irreducible polynomial $P$,
L73: 
L74:  | $$\overline{dc}(P)\geq\frac{{\rm dim}\;Z(P)^{*}+1}{2}.$$  |
L75: 
L76: Theorem cite27†1.0.3 is obtained by partially solving a question in classical algebraic geometry (Theorem cite28†2.3.1 ): find set-theoretic defining equations for the variety $Dual_{k,d,N}\subset\mathbb{P}(S^{d}\mathbb{C}^{N})$ of hypersurfaces of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{N-1}$ whose dual variety has dimension at most $k$.
L77: While it was generally understood that $\operatorname{End}(M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]\subset\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$ was a proper inclusion, it had not been known if the difference was potentially significant.
L78: Proposition cite29†3.5.1 exhibits an explicit codimension one $GL_{n^{2}}(\mathbb{C})$-orbit that is contained in the boundary of $\overline{GL_{n^{2}}\cdot[\operatorname{det}_{n}]}$ but not contained in $\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}})\cdot\operatorname{det}_{n}$, at least when $n$ is odd. In particular, we exhibit an explicit sequence of polynomials $P_{m}$ with $\overline{dc}(P_{m})<dc(P_{m})$.
L79: ## 2. Hypersurfaces with degenerate dual varieties
L80: ### 2.1. Katz’s dimension formula
L81: 
L82: Let $W$ be a complex vector space of dimension $N$, and $P\in S^{d}W^{*}$ a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$. Let $Z(P)\subset\mathbb{P}W$ denote the hypersurface defined by $P$. If $P$ is irreducible, then $Z(P)$ and its dual variety $Z(P)^{*}$, the Zariski closure of the set of tangent hyperplanes to $Z(P)$, are both irreducible. The Katz dimension formula [cite30†2 ] states that
L83: 
L84:  | $${\rm dim}\;Z(P)^{*}={\mathrm{rank}}(H_{P,w})-2,$$  |
L85: where $H_{P,w}$ denotes the Hessian of $P$ at $w$, a general point of the affine cone over $Z(P)$. Recall that the Hessian can be defined, once a coordinate system on $W$ has been chosen, as the symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives of $P$. Intrinsically, it is just the quadratic form constructed from $P$ by polarization:
L86: 
L87:  | $$H_{P,w}(X):=P(w,\ldots,w,X,X).$$  |
L88: Katz’s formula implies that $Z(P)^{*}$ has dimension less or equal to $k$ if and only if, for any $w\in W$ such that $P(w)=0$, and any $(k+3)$-dimensional subspace $F$ of $W$,
L89: 
L90:  | $$\det(H_{P,w}|_{F})=0.$$  |
L91: 
L92: Equivalently (assuming $P$ is irreducible), for any such subspace $F$, the polynomial $P$ must divide $\det(H_{P}|_{F})$, a polynomial of degree $(k+3)(d-2)$.
L93: ### 2.2. Pairs of polynomials such that one divides the other
L94: 
L95: Consider two homogeneous polynomials $P,Q$ on $W=\mathbb{C}^{N}$, of respective degrees $d,e$. We determine equations on their coefficients that are implied by the condition that $P$ divides $Q$.
L96: There is an obvious solution in the slightly different situation where $P$ and $Q$ are (non-homogeneous) polynomials in a single variable: one simply performs the Euclidian division of $Q$ by $P$ and requires that the remainder $R$ be zero. The ideal defined by this condition is described in [cite31†6 ].
L97: In our situation, we can first restrict $P$ and $Q$ to some plane $L$ in $W$, and choose coordinates $x,y$ on $L$. The restricted polynomials $P_{L}$ and $Q_{L}$ are then binary forms in these coordinates. Then set $y=1$ and perform a Euclidean division on the resulting polynomials in $x$. After rehomogenization, we obtain
L98: 
L99: (1)  |  | $$Q_{L}(x,y)=P_{L}(x,y)D_{L}(x,y)+y^{e-d+1}R_{L}(x,y),$$  |
L100: where $R_{L}(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $d-1$. The condition $R_{L}=0$ depends on the choice of the coordinates $x$ and $y$, but up to scale, the coefficient $R_{L,d-1}$ of $x^{d-1}$ only depends on the choice of the coordinate $y$. That is, the condition $R_{L,d-1}=0$, considered as a polynomial equation in the coefficients of $P$ and $Q$, only depends on the choice of $L$ and of the line $D$ in $L$ defined by the equation $y=0$.

L104: P_{L}(x,y)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}p_{j}x^{j}y^{d-j}=p_{d}\prod_{l=1}^{d}(x-y\beta_{l}).\end{array}$$  |
